[n.3] Shubi and Hangaza are historically Rundi dialects that the colonial partition left to Tanzania. new_statements.relation_note: Tone language of the Rwanda-Rundi type; no stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shubi has the Rwanda-Rundi lexical tone system: distinctive H tones with about five tonal patterns on disyllabic noun stems and two on disyllabic infinitives (the author's typology places such systems on the 'tonal' side, languages with 1<(a)<4 being 'accent' languages); nothing is said about word stress or a demarcative accent for Shubi.
new_statements.exceptions: Shubi carries a '?' in Tableau II (imperfectly known; scheme counts inferred from limited own notes); Ha only 'probably' and Vinza 'perhaps' share the system; no Shubi forms are cited in the thesis.
new_statements.identity_note: 'shubi (D 64)' listed in groupe II (Hautes Terres de l'Ouest) with rwanda D61, rundi D62, ha D66, hangaza D65, vinza D67 (Tableau 1, p.70); footnote p.412: 'Le shubi et le hangaza sont historiquement des dialectes rundi que le découpage colonial a laissés à la Tanzanie' = Shubi JD64 of Ngara (shub1238), not Subi [xsj] of Biharamulo. Data are the author's own field notes ('rwanda, ha, shubi et hangaza (groupe II)', Sources p.515), i.e. the Philippson recordings that Jouannet 1985 also used.

new_statements.identity_note: The snippet is a comparative feature table whose visible columns are '.. Shubi Hangaza Ruanda Rundi' (Nurse's West Highlands / Rwanda-Rundi group, in which 'Shubi' is the Ngara JD64 language of his TLS fieldwork = shub1238, not Subi xsj). The statement is a group-level row ('all have tones'), not a Shubi-specific analysis. Caveat: Google attributes the snippet to the Chaga volume (Buske 1979); the same author's group profiles also appear in Nurse 1979 (African Languages 5(1)) and Nurse & Philippson 1980, so the physical location of this table should be verified in print before citing a page.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources on placement: the only work, Seidel 1898, states penultimate word stress three times (p. 151 §2 vowel length in the stressed syllable; p. 152 §3 'Der Wortton ruht gewöhnlich auf der vorletzten Silbe'; p. 153 §4 m with examples yawatéra, akagúla, kulemíla) and mentions no tone. The conflict is one of language identity: the described variety (Ki-Sindja of Usindja, between Emin Pasha Gulf and Smith Sound, south shore of Lake Victoria) is Zinza JE23 per Glottolog and per the article's own locality statement, not Shubi JD64; the readall target assigns the work to Shubi on the strength of older bibliographies. Also note that a 1898 'Wortton' statement by a German officer-recorder for a Great Lakes Bantu language (the region's languages are tonal) is weak evidence for a stress system as such; it more likely reflects penultimate lengthening/prominence heard as stress.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Settles identity: Shubi [suj] is JD64, Ngara District, 'very similar to Hangaza [han]' and Rundi; Subi [xsj] is a different language (Biharamulo; close to Nyambo/Haya/Zinza, E.20). Mentions an SIL Tanzania sociolinguistic survey of Nyambo, Hangaza, Shubi, Subi and Sumbwa (May-June 2016) whose findings 'are presented so far in wordlists. The report is still in progress.'
